_comment: Following someone as they recite. The rules that use these numbers are in lib/recite/soundalike.js and lib/recite/follow.js; this file is only what the numbers are. Nothing here decides which engine listens: that is backend config, because the key and the model live there.
_comment-orange: Letters a microphone confuses with each other. Each line is one group, and any letter in a group counts as any other when deciding whether a word that came back wrong is a near miss rather than a mistake. This runs AFTER the spelling fold in arabicText.js, never instead of it: مَٰلِكِ and مالك are one word and must never reach this rule at all.
_comment-orange-why-wide: The groups are wider than a phonetics book would draw them, on purpose. Getting this wrong in one direction shows orange, which says 'I cannot tell whether you slipped or I misheard'. Getting it wrong in the other direction shows red, which tells a reciter they made a mistake they did not make. The first is honest, the second is a lie, so the doubt is drawn wide.
_comment-orange-groups: سصث the s sounds. تط and دضظذز the plain and emphatic pairs, which is where nearly every real confusion has been. قك the two k sounds. حهة the breath at the end of a word, where ة and ه are the same sound in pause. خغ. ءعئ the catch in the throat, dropped by every engine at some point. ؤو.
_comment-article: The ال at the front of a word is dropped by every engine at some point: real recitation came back as رحمن for ٱلرَّحْمَٰنِ, on a Groq reading, simply because the sound was cut there. A reciter dropping it is far rarer than a microphone losing it, so the pair counts as a near miss rather than a mistake. Only when enough word is left without it: ٱللَّهِ without its ال is لله, which is a different word anyone might really say, so a word that short keeps its ال and is judged whole.
_comment-costs: What each way of being wrong costs when lining up what was heard against what is on the page. Only the sizes relative to each other matter, and each one is a claim about the reciter, so what it costs is how strong a claim it is. A near miss costs almost nothing, so doubt always wins over an accusation, which is rule 2 said in numbers. A word said that is not in the book is the strongest claim of the four and costs the most: it must cost more than reading the same sound as the word it stood in for (5 against 4), or the last word of an ayah said wrongly is reported as a word added and a word never reached. And one wrong word must cost less than a word lost plus a word gained (4 against 3+5), so it is read as one mistake and not as two.
_repeat-look: How many heard words after a word gone back to may show the phrase going on from there (follow.js goesOn). One stray word equal to an earlier one is not a repeat: the next page's first word, or a wrong last word, pulled the reciter back up the page. Two, so one word the ear spelled oddly in a repeat does not hide it.
_cost-back: What it costs to go back to a word already reached and say it again, paid once per jump however long the phrase gone over. A reciter practising says a phrase over and over; with no way to go back, every repeat was read as wrong words further down the page. Less than one wrong word (4), so even one word said twice is a repeat; more than a near miss, so a word that lines up where it is still does.
_cost-split: What it costs to read two heard pieces as one word of the page. An engine cuts what it heard wherever the reciter paused, and a pause can land inside a word: العالمين came back as العالم then مين. That is the machine's doing and not the reciter's, so it must be readable as one word rather than as two mistakes. It is not free, so a word heard whole is still preferred, and it can only happen when the two pieces put together are the printed word, which is why so small a cost is safe.
_anchor-words: How many words of the page must be heard before anything at all is marked. Nothing on this page is worth saying until the reciter is actually on it: with music playing in the room the engine returned موسيقى, and every one of those words was lined up against the page and shown as twelve mistakes by somebody who had not yet said a word. One word could be a coincidence, so two.
_settle-words: How many words must go past before a word may be marked. Nothing is marked as it is said, because what the engine heard changes as it hears more: a word alone comes back wrong and comes back right once the words after it are in. Three is what the reciter sees as 'a moment later' rather than 'it changed its mind'.
_window-s: The longest a recording may run with no pause in it; a pause (pause-s) ends one sooner, and nearly always does. A cut on this clock lands mid-word and the word is lost from both recordings: at 10 seconds al-Fatihah 1:7, 14 seconds with no breath, lost الضالين every time. 25 keeps under the 30 seconds the ear reads at once. Shorter windows cut words in half, four seconds turned إياك نعبد into إيا كان عبوا.
_pause-s: A pause this long ends the recording early, so each one is a whole phrase and the next begins on a whole word. Measured with back-to-back ten-second windows and the strict ear: a perfect al-Fatihah showed 7 not said and 2 wrong, because a word cut at a window's edge is dropped as unsure and is never heard whole in any window. A reciter pauses at every ayah, so cutting there costs nothing. The meter sees about 0.7 seconds at a time, so this is on top of that.
_step-s: The least time between two requests, only a floor: how long the last reading actually took paces the rest, since one reading is in flight at a time, and the server's listen_per_minute (through asks-share) sets the ceiling.
_asks-share: The part of the server's listen_per_minute (its listening keys times 20) the page may spend, the same margin as asks-per-minute below said in a share: eighteen of twenty is 0.9. The page uses this on the server's count when it gives one, so a second key doubles the readings asked for.
_asks-per-minute: How many readings may be asked for in any sixty seconds when the server has not said how many its keys allow (see asks-share). Groq's free allowance is twenty; going over it rests the fast ear for listening_rest_s (sixty seconds). A reading at a pause is never held back, mid-phrase ones give way; eighteen leaves the pause readings their room.
_tick-s: How often the recording hands over what it has, which is how soon after the ear is free the next reading can start. Not how often a request is sent: a request is sent when the ear has answered and this much sound has arrived since the last one was asked for. Small costs nothing, the pieces are simply joined, and it is what turns a fixed wait into 'as soon as it can'.
_sure-at: How sure the ear must be, 0 to 1, that a page word is in the sound. Sureness is judged on sound, so it is the only thing here that hears a vowel: lining up words compares letters, and a wrong vowel keeps the same letters. A word the transcript found but the ear is less sure of than this is red; a word the transcript missed but the ear is at least this sure of counts as said. A word with no sureness (its recording did not place) is orange at worst, never red. One level, no toggle: either the word was said right or it was not. Measured with backend/scripts/recitation/sweep_sureness.py, forgiving a word's single worst piece: at 0.95, on 795 right words in clean recordings 2.9% were marked red and 67% of vowel slips were caught (letters ear: 4.7% and 66%). 0.9 caught 60% for 2.1%, 0.97 69% for 3.3%, 0.99 71% for 4.8%; judging by the single worst piece caught 86% but marked 10-12% of right words red. Fewer false marks and more catches are the same dial. Tajweed is not judged.
_keep-recordings: How many of the latest recordings the page keeps in memory so a word card can play back what a mark was judged from. Each is a few seconds of compressed sound, up to window-s long; twelve is about three pages of ayahs, and the oldest is dropped past it.
_journal-heard-chars: How much of what the ear wrote goes into the journal's reading note. A long recording writes a few hundred letters; the cap keeps one reading from filling the journal's page allowance.
_comment-silence: How quiet counts as silence is not here: it is voice-level in dictation.json, already read by the microphone button, and one idea of 'nobody is speaking' is enough for the app. A window under it is never sent, because a silent one costs the engine on this machine up to seventeen seconds and returns nothing.
_check-timeout-s: The longest a sureness check may take before it is given up on. Without one, a request that never answers left checkBusy stuck true forever and nothing after it in the queue was ever sent.
_check-queue-max: The most sureness checks held waiting to be sent. Past it the oldest not-yet-sent one is dropped to make room; the one already in flight is never touched.
_journal-flush-ms: How often lib/recite/journal.js sends whatever it is holding, if reciting has not already filled a batch.
_journal-batch: How many events lib/recite/journal.js sends in one call, and the queue length that triggers an early flush rather than waiting for journal-flush-ms. The backend accepts up to 50 per call; well under that leaves room for a burst mid-flush.
_journal-queue-max: The most events lib/recite/journal.js holds before it starts dropping the newest rather than growing without bound. A crash worth reading about is not a crash worth running out of memory for first.
_sound-letters: How the sounds ear's symbols are written back as Arabic for the word card (lib/recite/sounds.js). A doubled symbol is its letter with a shadda; vowels are harakat, a long one adds its letter. Tajweed-only symbols are written as their plain letter.
